title: Innovation Prototyping
summary: Sanitized experiments that turn uncertain ideas into scenes, interactions, and visual systems people can evaluate early—bridging generative art direction with the same spatial and visualization instincts used in shipped AR and data work.
role: Creative technologist and software engineer — concept framing, UI, real-time prototypes, generative workflows, and decision journals
problem: Innovation teams need enough fidelity to feel a future experience, but enough flexibility to change direction before a concept becomes expensive—whether the next artifact is a storyboard, a WebGL scene, a map encoding, or a generated keyframe.
constraints: Client and employer-specific material remains abstracted or removed.
Generated imagery needs deliberate art direction, privacy review, and traceable iteration.
Spatial and visualization depth for event AR, WebXR, and newsroom graphics lives in dedicated sibling stories; this story focuses on the decision-framed pipeline.
The August launch focuses on one strong Manhattan 2150 proof scene; a full six-shot film remains post-launch scope.
approach: Frame each prototype around the decision it needs to unlock—try-on feel, narrative beat, encoding clarity—not around a preferred tool.
Move between storyboard, interface sketch, real-time scene, map or diagram, and generated image without treating any one artifact as the final truth.
Reuse spatial laboratory habits (Three.js wireframes, helix and tesseract motion) and visualization literacy (SVG encodings, network metaphors) so generative work stays grounded in systems thinking.
Record prompt and composition decisions in a sanitized journal so iteration is inspectable.
Package the strongest shot and six-frame storyboard as evidence of a repeatable creative pipeline that can hand off to production AR or product UX.
